analogy.p: Think of a shopping centre with an up escalator and a down escalator between two floors. People travelling up are like the forward reaction and people travelling down are like the reverse reaction. When the numbers on each floor stay constant, the same number of people are going up as down, even though everyone is still moving. That is dynamic equilibrium. If the ground floor gets crowded (more reactant), more people go up, and if you take people away from the top floor (remove ammonia), more go up to replace them. The analogy breaks down because people choose where to go, while molecules react by chance collisions.
analogy.t: A busy escalator and a crowd

bullets: Product: **ammonia, NH3**, used mainly to make **fertilisers** (and also nitric acid, explosives and cleaning products).
Raw materials: **nitrogen** (from the air) and **hydrogen** (from natural gas, which is mainly methane).
The reaction is **reversible**, so the product mixture also contains unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen.
It needs an **iron catalyst**, a temperature of about **450 °C** and a pressure of about **200 atmospheres**.
Higher tier: you must **explain why** these conditions are chosen using ideas of equilibrium, rate, yield, cost and energy.
The process is a good example of balancing **chemistry (yield and rate)** against **economics (cost and energy)**.
Spec link: this sits alongside reversible reactions, dynamic equilibrium and the rates of reaction topics.
core.h: What the Haber process makes and why it matters
core.p: The **Haber process** is the industrial method for making **ammonia (NH3)** from nitrogen and hydrogen. Ammonia is one of the most important chemicals in the world because it is the starting material for **fertilisers**, which allow farmers to grow enough food for the world's population. The process was developed by Fritz Haber and scaled up by Carl Bosch in the early twentieth century. The key difficulty is that the reaction is **reversible**, so a great deal of chemistry is used to get a good yield of ammonia at a reasonable speed and cost.

bullets: Equation: **N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3**.
Forward reaction (making ammonia) is **exothermic**: ΔH is about −92 kJ per mole of the equation as written.
Reverse reaction (breaking ammonia down) is **endothermic** by the same amount.
Left side: **4 moles of gas**; right side: **2 moles of gas**.
The ⇌ sign shows the reaction can go **both ways** in the same reaction mixture.
The reaction never goes to completion in a single pass: some nitrogen and hydrogen always remain.
core.p: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia. The reaction is **reversible**, shown by the sign ⇌ in the equation, and the forward reaction is **exothermic**, meaning it releases heat to the surroundings. This means the reverse reaction (ammonia breaking down into nitrogen and hydrogen) is **endothermic**. The balanced equation shows that **1 mole of nitrogen reacts with 3 moles of hydrogen to make 2 moles of ammonia**, so 4 moles of gas turn into 2 moles of gas. This reduction in the number of gas molecules is the key to understanding the effect of pressure.

bullets: **Nitrogen from the air** (about 78% nitrogen), separated by fractional distillation of liquid air.
**Hydrogen from natural gas** (methane), by reaction with steam.
The gases are mixed in the **1 : 3 ratio** of nitrogen to hydrogen by volume, matching the equation.
Both raw materials are **abundant and cheap**, which makes the process economical.
The air is a renewable source of nitrogen; natural gas is a finite fossil fuel, a sustainability issue.
Hydrogen could instead come from **water by electrolysis**, which can be used with renewable electricity (extension).
core.h: Where the raw materials come from
core.p: The raw materials are cheap and plentiful. **Nitrogen** makes up about 78% of the air, so it is obtained from the **air** by fractional distillation of liquid air. **Hydrogen** is obtained from **natural gas**, which is mostly methane. The methane is reacted with steam at high temperature in the presence of a catalyst, which produces hydrogen. The nitrogen and hydrogen are mixed in the ratio of 1 : 3 by volume, which matches the balanced equation. Because the reactants are cheap, the main costs of the process are energy and the building and running of the plant.

bullets: 1. **Purify and mix** nitrogen and hydrogen in a 1 : 3 ratio.
2. **Compress** the gas to about **200 atm** (high pressure).
3. Pass over an **iron catalyst** at about **450 °C** in the reactor.
4. **Cool** the gas leaving the reactor: ammonia has a much higher boiling point so it **liquefies**.
5. **Remove liquid ammonia** and store it.
6. **Recycle** unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen back to the reactor.
The ammonia can be separated because its boiling point (about −33 °C) is much higher than those of nitrogen (−196 °C) and hydrogen (−253 °C).
Recycling is essential because only a **fraction** of the gases reacts on each pass through the reactor.
core.p: The mixture of nitrogen and hydrogen is **compressed** to about 200 atmospheres and **heated** to about 450 °C. It then passes over an **iron catalyst** in the reactor, where some of it is converted to ammonia. Because the reaction is reversible, the gases leaving the reactor are a mixture of ammonia, nitrogen and hydrogen. This mixture is **cooled**, which causes the **ammonia to condense into a liquid** and be removed. The **unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen** remain as gases and are **recycled** back into the reactor, so that nothing is wasted and a high overall conversion is achieved.

bullets: Reversible reaction: A + B ⇌ C + D; products can turn back into reactants.
Forward and reverse reactions occur at the same time in the same container.
If the reaction is **exothermic in one direction**, it is **endothermic in the opposite direction**, and the energy change is the same size.
Example from the spec: the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride (reversible) and hydrated copper sulfate (reversible), where heating and cooling reverse the change.
For equilibrium to be reached the system must be **closed**.
Some reactions are not reversible, they only go one way (for example burning).
Reversibility is why the Haber process does not give 100% yield.
core.p: A **reversible reaction** is one in which the products can react to re-form the original reactants. In the Haber process the nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia, but ammonia also decomposes to nitrogen and hydrogen. In an **open system** the products escape and the reaction goes to completion. In a **closed system** (nothing can enter or leave) the forward and reverse reactions both continue until a state of **dynamic equilibrium** is reached. Chemically the equation is written with the two-way arrow ⇌.

bullets: At equilibrium: **rate of forward reaction = rate of reverse reaction**.
Concentrations of reactants and products are **constant**, not necessarily equal.
Both reactions are **still occurring**: that is why it is called **dynamic**.
It can only be reached in a **closed system**.
The **position of equilibrium** tells you the relative amounts of reactants and products: to the right means more products; to the left means more reactants.
At equilibrium there is no overall change in the appearance or composition of the mixture.
A graph of rate against time shows the forward rate falling and the reverse rate rising until they meet.
core.p: When a reversible reaction takes place in a **closed system**, the forward reaction starts fast because there is a lot of reactant, and the reverse reaction starts slowly because there is no product yet. As reactants are used up the forward rate falls, and as products build up the reverse rate increases. Eventually the **rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction**. This state is called **dynamic equilibrium**. It is dynamic because both reactions are still happening, but the **concentrations of reactants and products stay constant**. The reaction has not stopped.

bullets: Statement: if a change is made to conditions, the system **responds to counteract the change**.
**Increase concentration** of a reactant: equilibrium shifts to **use up** that reactant, so more product forms.
**Decrease concentration** of a product (by removing it): equilibrium shifts to make **more product**.
**Increase pressure**: equilibrium shifts towards the side with **fewer gas molecules**.
**Increase temperature**: equilibrium shifts in the **endothermic** direction (which takes in heat).
**Decrease temperature**: equilibrium shifts in the **exothermic** direction (which gives out heat).
A **catalyst** does **not** change the position of equilibrium.
core.p: **Le Chatelier's principle** states that if a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to **counteract the change**. This allows us to predict how the position of equilibrium shifts when the concentration, pressure or temperature is changed. If the change is made, the equilibrium moves in the direction that opposes it, and a new equilibrium is established. You must apply this to the Haber process to explain why the conditions are chosen.

bullets: Forward reaction exothermic, so **higher temperature → equilibrium shifts left → lower yield of NH3**.
**Lower temperature → shifts right → higher yield**.
But at low temperatures the **rate of reaction is very slow**, so equilibrium would take too long to reach.
Higher temperature increases the **rate** because particles have more energy and collide more often and more successfully.
This conflict between yield and rate means a **compromise** temperature is chosen: **450 °C**.
On a graph of yield against temperature, the line **slopes downwards**.
Do not say the temperature is raised to get more ammonia: it is raised to get ammonia **faster**.
core.h: Effect of temperature on the Haber process (Higher tier)
core.p: The forward reaction is exothermic. If the temperature is **increased**, the system responds by opposing the change, shifting in the **endothermic direction** to take in heat. This is the reverse reaction, so the equilibrium moves to the **left** and the **yield of ammonia decreases**. If the temperature is **decreased**, the equilibrium shifts to the **right** (the exothermic direction), so the yield increases. Therefore, to get the highest yield of ammonia, a **low temperature** would be best.

bullets: More moles of gas on the left (**4**) than on the right (**2**).
**Increase pressure → equilibrium shifts right → higher yield** of ammonia.
Higher pressure also gives a **faster rate** because particles are closer together and collide more often.
Reasons not to use extremely high pressure: **cost of strong pipes and reaction vessels**, **cost of energy** for compression, and **safety risks** (leaks and explosions).
200 atm is a **compromise** between yield and cost.
On a graph of yield against pressure, the line **slopes upwards**.
If the numbers of gas molecules were equal on both sides, pressure would have no effect on the position.
core.h: Effect of pressure on the Haber process (Higher tier)
core.p: In the equation N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 there are **4 moles of gas on the left** and **2 moles of gas on the right**. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with **fewer gas molecules**, because that reduces the pressure and opposes the change. This is the **right-hand side**, so a **higher pressure gives a higher yield of ammonia**. High pressure also increases the **rate** because the gas particles are closer together, so they collide more frequently. However, very high pressure is expensive and dangerous, which is why 200 atm is a compromise.

bullets: Catalyst used: **iron**.
A catalyst provides an **alternative pathway with lower activation energy**.
It speeds up **both** the forward and reverse reactions equally.
It does **not** change the **position of equilibrium** or the **equilibrium yield**.
It lets the process work at a **lower temperature** than would otherwise be needed, which saves energy and costs.
Catalysts are **not used up** in the reaction.
**Concentration**: removing ammonia by liquefying it and adding more nitrogen and hydrogen both push the equilibrium to the right, giving more ammonia overall.
core.p: A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction without being used up. In the Haber process **iron** is used. A catalyst works by providing an **alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy**, so more collisions are successful. In a reversible reaction a catalyst speeds up the **forward and reverse reactions equally**, so it helps the system **reach equilibrium faster** but does **not change the position of equilibrium or the yield**. Without a catalyst the reaction would be too slow at 450 °C to be economical. The catalyst is cheap, lasts a long time and does not need to be replaced often.

bullets: **450 °C**: compromise between low yield at high temperatures and slow rate at low temperatures.
**200 atm**: high enough for a good yield and rate, but not so high that equipment and energy costs are excessive.
**Iron catalyst**: increases rate without affecting yield.
**Recycling** unreacted gases and **removing ammonia** as a liquid increase the overall yield.
The reaction is **exothermic**, so heat given out can be used to **heat the incoming gases**, saving energy.
Reasons for the compromise are always about **rate, yield, cost and safety**.
Economic factors include the cost of **energy**, **equipment**, **raw materials** and the **value of the product**.
core.h: Choosing the conditions: a compromise (Higher tier)
core.p: The best conditions for the process must balance **yield**, **rate** and **cost**. Low temperature gives a high yield but a rate that is too slow, so the plant would produce very little ammonia per day. High temperature gives a fast rate but the yield becomes too low. The compromise of **450 °C** gives an acceptable rate and a reasonable yield. A high pressure gives both a higher yield and a faster rate, but is expensive and hazardous, so **200 atm** is used. The **iron catalyst** speeds up the reaction so that it is economical at this moderate temperature.

bullets: Compressors and heaters use a lot of **energy**, which is a major running cost.
**Heat exchangers** use the heat released by the exothermic reaction to preheat incoming gas.
High pressure needs **thick-walled steel vessels and pipes**, which are costly.
Hydrogen is **flammable** and explosive, so leaks are a safety risk.
Ammonia is **toxic**, so it is stored and transported carefully.
The plant runs **continuously** as a continuous process so output is high and labour costs are low.
Sustainability: using natural gas and a lot of energy produces carbon dioxide; renewable hydrogen is being developed.
core.p: Industrial processes are designed to make money while keeping people safe and limiting damage to the environment. In the Haber process the largest costs are the **energy** needed to compress gases, the energy to heat the reactor and the **capital cost** of strong equipment that can withstand high pressures. Because the reaction is exothermic, the heat released is recycled using **heat exchangers**, reducing the energy needed. Safety is important because hydrogen is flammable and the gases are at high pressure. Ammonia is toxic and corrosive, so leaks must be avoided.

bullets: Ammonia + nitric acid → **ammonium nitrate**; ammonia + sulfuric acid → **ammonium sulfate**.
These salts are fertilisers because they provide **soluble nitrogen** for plants.
Fertilisers raise crop **yield** and are essential for food production.
Excess fertiliser washed into rivers causes **eutrophication**: algae bloom, oxygen is used up and fish die.
Other uses: **nitric acid**, explosives, nylon, cleaning products and refrigerants.
Compare: the NPK fertilisers topic (chem.9.6) covers nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium together.
The Haber process is therefore linked to **sustainable food production** and **environmental issues**.
core.h: Uses of ammonia and the link to fertilisers
core.p: Most ammonia is used to make **nitrogen-containing fertilisers**. Plants need nitrogen to make proteins, but they can only take it up as dissolved compounds such as nitrates and ammonium salts. Ammonia reacts with acids to make ammonium salts such as **ammonium nitrate** and **ammonium sulfate**, which are used as fertilisers. Fertilisers increase crop yields, which helps feed the growing population, but the extra nitrate that is washed off fields can pollute water and cause **eutrophication**. Ammonia is also used to make nitric acid, explosives, plastics and cleaning products.

bullets: Describe a graph: say what happens to yield **as** temperature (or pressure) **increases**, using values from the graph.
Explain the trend with **Le Chatelier**: exothermic forward → higher temperature lowers yield; fewer gas molecules on the right → higher pressure raises yield.
Volumes of gases react in ratio **N2 : H2 : NH3 = 1 : 3 : 2** (same temperature and pressure).
Mass: **28 g of N2 → 34 g of NH3** (Mr N2 = 28, Mr NH3 = 17).
Percentage yield = **actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100**.
Always check that units agree (for example kg with kg).
Use the **higher tier command words** carefully: 'explain' needs the reason, not only the trend.
core.p: Exam questions often give a graph of **percentage yield against temperature or pressure** for different conditions. You must read values carefully and describe the trend, then explain it using Le Chatelier's principle. For calculations you can use the balanced equation: gases react in the **ratio of their moles**, and at the same temperature and pressure equal moles of gas occupy equal volumes (Higher tier), so volumes react in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2. You can also use relative formula masses to calculate masses of ammonia produced and percentage yield.

exam: 1 mark: write the equation: **N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3**, balanced, with the ⇌ sign.
1 mark each: state the conditions: **iron catalyst, about 450 °C, about 200 atm**.
2 marks: where the raw materials come from: **nitrogen from the air, hydrogen from natural gas**.
2 marks: describe how ammonia is separated: the mixture is **cooled**, ammonia **liquefies** and is removed, unreacted gases are **recycled**.
2 marks: define dynamic equilibrium: **forward and reverse reactions at the same rate, concentrations constant** (in a closed system).

3 marks (Higher): explain the effect of temperature: forward reaction exothermic, so increasing temperature shifts equilibrium **left**, lowering the yield; but rate is slower at low temperatures, so a compromise is used.
3 marks (Higher): explain the effect of pressure: **4 moles of gas → 2 moles of gas**, so higher pressure shifts equilibrium right, increasing yield.
Always state **both** the effect on yield (equilibrium position) and the effect on rate when explaining conditions.
6 marks: use paragraph structure: temperature, pressure, catalyst, then cost and safety, and finish with a clear statement that conditions are a compromise.
Graph questions: quote **data from the graph** (for example yield at 450 °C and 200 atm) and then explain.
Calculations: use the **1 : 3 : 2** ratio for volumes, and **28 g N2 → 34 g NH3** for masses. Show every step.

mistakes.r: At dynamic equilibrium both reactions continue at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant.
The concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.
mistakes.w: At equilibrium the amounts of reactants and products are equal.

mistakes.r: A catalyst speeds up the rate only; it does not change the position of equilibrium or yield.
mistakes.w: The iron catalyst increases the yield of ammonia.

mistakes.r: Higher temperature lowers the yield because the forward reaction is exothermic; it is used to increase the rate.
mistakes.w: A high temperature is used to get a higher yield.

mistakes.r: Higher pressure does increase yield, but 200 atm is a compromise because higher pressures cost too much and are less safe.
mistakes.w: A very high pressure is used because it gives the best yield.

mistakes.r: Nitrogen comes from the air; hydrogen comes from natural gas (methane).
mistakes.w: Ammonia is made from nitrogen and hydrogen from the air.

mistakes.r: They are recycled back into the reactor.
Ammonia is cooled until it liquefies and is separated as a liquid, because its boiling point is higher than nitrogen and hydrogen.

summary: You must describe the Haber process: nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas react over an iron catalyst at about 450 °C and 200 atmospheres in a reversible reaction, with cooling to liquefy ammonia and recycling of unreacted gases. At Higher tier you must explain the conditions using dynamic equilibrium, Le Chatelier's principle, yield, rate, cost and energy. It matters because it links reversible reactions, rates and industrial chemistry.

terms.d: The industrial process for making ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst, about 450 °C and about 200 atmospheres.
A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the original reactants, shown by ⇌.
A system in which no substances can enter or leave.
The state in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the concentrations stay constant.
The relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium.
If a system at equilibrium is changed, the system responds to counteract the change.
A reaction that transfers energy (heat) to the surroundings.
A reaction that takes in energy (heat) from the surroundings.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
The amount of product obtained from a reaction.
Actual yield divided by theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
Returning unreacted reactants to the reactor so they can react again.
Conditions chosen to balance rate, yield, cost and safety.
NH3, a gas made in the Haber process, used mainly to make fertilisers.
A substance added to soil to provide elements such as nitrogen that plants need for growth.
The minimum energy that particles need to react when they collide.
A device that transfers heat from hot gases leaving the reactor to cooler gases entering it.

worked.ans: 200 dm3 of nitrogen is needed and 400 dm3 of ammonia is formed.
worked.q: At constant temperature and pressure, 600 dm3 of hydrogen reacts completely with nitrogen in the Haber process. Calculate the volume of nitrogen needed and the volume of ammonia formed. (3 marks)
steps: Equation: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, so volumes react in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2.

worked.ans: Theoretical mass = 17 kg of ammonia; percentage yield = 75%.
worked.q: Calculate the mass of ammonia that can be made from 14 kg of nitrogen. In a plant 12.75 kg of ammonia was actually made. Calculate the percentage yield. (4 marks) (Ar: N = 14, H = 1)
steps: Mr of N2 = 28; Mr of NH3 = 17.
N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3: 28 g of N2 makes 2 × 17 = 34 g of NH3.
14 kg of N2 makes 14 × 34/28 = 17 kg of NH3 (theoretical yield).

worked.ans: 450 °C balances a reasonable rate against a falling yield (exothermic forward reaction); 200 atm increases yield and rate (4 → 2 moles of gas) without excessive cost and safety risks; the iron catalyst increases the rate only. The unreacted gases are recycled and ammonia is liquefied and removed to improve the overall yield.
worked.q: Explain why the Haber process uses a temperature of 450 °C and a pressure of 200 atmospheres. (6 marks)
steps: Temperature: the forward reaction is exothermic, so a lower temperature would give a higher yield of ammonia at equilibrium; but the rate would be too slow.
So 450 °C is a compromise: fast enough with the iron catalyst, with an acceptable yield.
Pressure: there are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so high pressure shifts equilibrium right and increases yield, and also increases the rate.
But very high pressure needs thick, expensive equipment, uses more energy and is dangerous, so 200 atm is a compromise.
The iron catalyst speeds up the reaction without changing the yield, allowing a lower temperature to be used.
